flawed_step: 0060–0065: From R_{m-1} having no neighbors in W_m and R_{m-1}⊆S, the proof incorrectly concludes that S has no neighbors in W_m. Added vertices in S\R_{m-1} may have such neighbors; also S⊆W_{m-1} does not imply S∩W_m=∅ because the W_i need not be disjoint.
counterexample: Let n=6, α=1/3, V={1,2,3,4,5,6}, and let G be K5 on {2,3,4,5,6} with vertex 1 isolated. This graph satisfies the hypothesis: every 3-vertex set contains at least two K5 vertices, so its neighbor set is {2,3,4,5,6}, of size 5=n/2+αn. Take W_{m-1}={1,2,3,4}, W_m={2,3,4,5,6}, and R_{m-1}={1}. Then R_{m-1} has no neighbor in W_m and |R_{m-1}|<n/2. The prescribed extension may be S={1,2,3}. But 2∈S is adjacent to 4∈W_m, so N(S)∩W_m≠∅; indeed N(S)={2,3,4,5,6}. Thus N(S)⊆V\W_m is false.
assessment_summary: The base-case argument essentially works, but the inductive contradiction fails in its small-reachable-set case. Nonadjacency of R_{m-1} to W_m does not extend to an arbitrary superset S, so the expansion contradiction is not established.
